sources.title: Memorandum of Agreement for Cooperative Management of Customary and Traditional Subsistence Uses in the Ahtna Region
sources.publisher: U.S. Department of the Interior / Ahtna Inter-Tribal Resource Commission
sources.annotation: Read the operative text on PDF pp.1–8 of the twenty-page document. The 2016 agreement sets out partnership goals, proposed rulemaking, knowledge-sharing and a proposed advisory process. Its general provisions retain federal responsibilities and say it creates no enforceable obligations or rights. Appended signature pages and map are not separate sources. Later implementation needs its own evidence.

sources.title: Community Harvest System Report, 2023–2025
sources.author: Deanna Kosbruk and Jim Simon
sources.annotation: Read all eight pages; visually checked the participation summary and chart on pp.5–6. January 2026 account of administration, eligibility, hunting effort and recommendations. Some chart percentages and reported averages conflict with the narrative counts; those rates are not repeated. Outcomes concern this federal program during 2023–2025, not every Ahtna hunt. Proposed regulatory changes are recommendations, not demonstrated later decisions.

sources.title: Copper River Salmon Health Surveillance
sources.annotation: Read the substantive project text, sampling design, community participation and laboratory-method sections. This undated page describes work illustrated by 2023–2025 activity. It supplies a substantial account of community-led monitoring and partnerships. Preliminary sampled-fish observations do not establish watershed-wide prevalence, a causal explanation for salmon declines, or food-safety advice. Images and linked pages are not extra counted works.

sources.title: Traditional Knowledge of Changes in Winter Conditions in Alaska’s Copper River Basin
sources.publisher: Alaska Park Science 22(1):90–101 / National Park Service, with Ahtna Intertribal Resource Commission
sources.author: Odin Miller
sources.annotation: Read the complete 2023 article, methods, participant table, interviews, conclusions and acknowledgments. Abridges a technical report, which is not separately counted. Nine purposively selected interviews include Ahtna, Upper Tanana and other regional residents. Their accounts connect environmental and socioeconomic changes, with differing experiences. Historical travel descriptions and crossing maps are not current safety guidance or public-access routes.

proposedParagraphs.title: Cooperative wildlife management
proposedParagraphs.text: A 2016 agreement between the Interior Department and AITRC identifies a shared purpose: sustaining wildlife and opportunities to continue customary subsistence practices. It provides a framework for rulemaking, cooperative research and an advisory process, with Ahtna knowledge contributing to management decisions. The document also retains federal responsibilities, makes proposed actions conditional on applicable procedures, and states that it creates no enforceable obligations or rights. Reading those provisions together shows a negotiated process whose implementation must be traced through later decisions, rather than assuming that signing the agreement transferred land or complete wildlife authority.

proposedParagraphs.title: What a community harvest program records
proposedParagraphs.text: Kosbruk and Simon’s January 2026 report follows the Community Harvest System through administration, registration, hunting effort and participants’ feedback. It describes pooled harvest opportunities under a federal framework and explains the inclusion of federally qualified rural residents of the named communities. For 2023–2025, its moose-program summaries report no successful harvests, alongside continuing outreach and coordination. This is a bounded account of one program, not a measure of all Ahtna hunting or food sharing. The authors connect access, competition and environmental conditions with participants’ difficulties and advocate regulatory changes; that advocacy does not establish what later regulators decided.

proposedParagraphs.title: Community questions and salmon research
proposedParagraphs.text: AITRC’s salmon-health account connects fishers’ observations with a research program involving tissue samples, measurements and laboratory work. Sampling across locations and portions of the run helps examine variation that a single collection could miss. Working with people already harvesting salmon links monitoring to community food priorities and practical knowledge of the river. The project is described as preliminary surveillance with partner laboratories and federal support. Its sampled observations provide a starting point for continued investigation; they cannot establish every fish’s condition or explain salmon trends across other watersheds.

proposedParagraphs.title: Winter travel, knowledge and changing conditions
proposedParagraphs.text: Miller’s collaborative study brings regional residents’ experiences into an account of changing winter access. Interviewees describe later or less reliable river ice, variable snow and effects on trapping, firewood gathering and travel. Their observations differ, and the nine interviews were selected for experience rather than as a population survey. Ahtna elders’ accounts appear alongside Upper Tanana and other residents’ testimony. The article also examines wage employment, settlement and changing transport technology. Those connections show why environmental change belongs within a wider history of work and access, while historical descriptions cannot establish safe crossing places today.

researchGaps: Follow particular regulatory recommendations through later decisions before making any current eligibility, season or harvest-limit claim.
Community Harvest System chart percentages and some averages require clarification against their underlying records. Do not silently repair or reuse them.
Compare additional community-authored experiences of food sharing and access; one program's harvest records are not a regional food census.
The winter article's underlying technical report is a related version, not an additional counted work unless genuinely new distinct evidence warrants separate treatment.
